Epidemiology & Risk Factors.title: Lung Cancer: Epidemiology & Risk Factors
Epidemiology & Risk Factors.html:
Lung cancer is the deadliest cancer in the United States and the second most commonly diagnosed cancer overall (not counting skin cancer). Understanding who develops it, and why, is the foundation for everything that follows in staging and treatment, a patient's smoking history, histology, and even sex can completely change the management pathway.

The Scope of the Problem

Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the US, and the 2nd most common cancer diagnosed (excluding skin cancers). A fact that surprises many students: roughly 20% of lung cancers occur in patients with no smoking history at all. This nonsmoking-associated population is clinically distinct, they are more likely to be female, more likely to develop adenocarcinoma rather than squamous cell carcinoma, and more likely to carry a targetable driver mutation.

Two Diseases Under One Name: NSCLC vs. SCLC

"Lung cancer" is really two very different diseases lumped under one umbrella term. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the more common of the two and includes adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and less common histologies like large cell carcinoma and carcinoid. Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) makes up only about 10-15% of cases but behaves very differently: it is a high-grade neuroendocrine tumor, it is almost always associated with a smoking history, and it is far more aggressive, with a strong tendency toward early distant failure and brain metastases. This underlying biological difference is exactly why SCLC gets its own simplified staging framework (limited vs. extensive stage, covered in the Workup & Staging doc) instead of being managed purely off the TNM grid.

Within NSCLC, adenocarcinoma is the single most common histology overall (~40% of all lung cancers), tends to arise peripherally, and accounts for most nonsmoking-associated cases. Squamous cell carcinoma makes up about 20% of lung cancers and classically arises centrally, near the mainstem bronchi.

Who Gets Lung Cancer: Risk Factors

Smoking remains the dominant risk factor, but it is not the only one. Other established risk factors include radon exposure, asbestos, a family history of lung cancer, underlying pulmonary fibrosis, and occupational exposures, silica, cadmium, arsenic, beryllium, diesel exhaust, and coal soot are all recognized carcinogens for lung cancer.

Clinical Pearl A young, nonsmoking woman with lung adenocarcinoma is a classic exam scenario. This population has a disproportionately high rate of EGFR mutations: a targetable driver mutation (treated with osimertinib) that is also associated with an improved prognosis relative to EGFR-wild-type disease.

Screening for Early Detection

Because most lung cancers are asymptomatic until locally advanced, screening high-risk patients with low-dose CT (LDCT) is a major public health strategy. The pivotal trial was the National Lung Cancer Screening Trial (NLST), which randomized patients to annual LDCT versus chest X-ray and found a 20% relative reduction in lung cancer mortality with LDCT (NEJM 2011). Based on this and subsequent data, the USPSTF recommends annual LDCT for adults ages 50-80 with at least a 20 pack-year smoking history who are either current smokers or who quit within the last 15 years.

How Lung Cancer Presents

Presentation varies enormously depending on a tumor's stage and location. Many cancers are now caught incidentally on screening CT before any symptoms develop. When symptomatic, patients may present with cough, shortness of breath, hoarseness (from recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement), chest pain, unintentional weight loss, pleural effusion, or post-obstructive pneumonia from a bronchus-occluding central tumor. Some patients instead present with symptoms from a distant metastasis, for example, headaches or focal neurologic deficits from a brain metastasis.

Lung cancers can also produce paraneoplastic syndromes: remote effects driven by tumor-secreted substances rather than local tumor bulk. These histology-specific pairings are classic and testable:

  • Squamous cell carcinoma → hypercalcemia, from tumor secretion of PTH-related peptide (PTHrP)
  • SCLC → SIADH, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, and paraneoplastic cerebellar ataxia (reflecting SCLC's neuroendocrine origin)
Clinical Pearl Match the paraneoplastic syndrome to the histology: squamous cell carcinoma → hypercalcemia (PTHrP); SCLC → SIADH, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, or cerebellar ataxia. These pairings reflect real underlying tumor biology, squamous cells can produce a PTH-like peptide, while SCLC's neuroendocrine nature drives antibody-mediated paraneoplastic phenomena.

Anatomy & Lymphatics.title: Mediastinal & Hilar Lymph Node Anatomy
Anatomy & Lymphatics.html:
Where a lung cancer's lymph nodes are involved matters just as much as the size of the primary tumor, it is often the single biggest factor separating a patient who can be cured with local therapy alone from one who needs a completely different treatment strategy. Thoracic clinicians organize the mediastinum into numbered lymph node "stations" using a shared map (the IASLC nodal station classification), and this map is the single most important diagram in thoracic oncology to understand cold.

The Numbering System: A Quick Rule of Thumb

The easiest way to remember the station map is by counting digits:

  • Single-digit stations (2-9) are mediastinal nodes.
  • Double-digit stations (10-14) are hilar and intrapulmonary nodes.
  • Station 1 is the low cervical/supraclavicular region.

This single rule lets you translate a station number directly into an N-stage: involvement of an ipsilateral hilar node (10-14) is N1 disease (stage IIB); involvement of an ipsilateral mediastinal node, including the subcarinal station (2-9), is N2 disease (stage IIIA); and involvement of contralateral mediastinal or hilar nodes, or supraclavicular nodes (station 1), is N3 disease (stage IIIB or IIIC).

The Station Map

Why Station 7 (Subcarinal) Matters So Much

Station 7, the subcarinal node, sits directly beneath the tracheal bifurcation (the carina) and receives lymphatic drainage from both lungs. Because either lung can drain into it, station 7 is the single most commonly involved mediastinal station in lung cancer, and it is treated as ipsilateral N2 disease no matter which lung the primary tumor sits in. Its central position, wedged between the esophagus, both mainstem bronchi, and the heart, also makes it critical for radiation planning: it is almost always encompassed in the treatment volume for locally advanced disease, and its proximity to the esophagus is a major driver of esophagitis risk during concurrent chemoradiation.

A Built-In Trap: Stations 5 and 6

Stations 5 (subaortic/aortopulmonary window) and 6 (para-aortic) are left-sided nodal stations by definition: they simply do not exist on the right side of the mediastinum. This creates a classic staging trap: if a patient has a right-sided primary tumor and imaging shows nodal disease at station 5 or 6, that finding is automatically contralateral spread and is staged as N3 disease, even though a student might be tempted to call it N2 because it still looks "mediastinal."

Hilar vs. Mediastinal: Why the Distinction Drives Management

The hilar/mediastinal boundary is not just nomenclature, it reflects a real anatomic and prognostic dividing line. Hilar (N1) disease is still resectable with a standard lobectomy and lymph node dissection, and surgery remains a reasonable first option. Once disease crosses into the mediastinum (N2), the calculus changes: patients often need multidisciplinary discussion about induction therapy, and bulky or multi-station N2 disease pushes management toward definitive chemoradiation rather than surgery (see Treatment Paradigms). During surgical resection, current practice calls for routine nodal mapping, at minimum one N1 station and three N2 stations should be sampled (or a complete lymph node dissection performed), and if N2 disease is found intraoperatively, a formal ipsilateral mediastinal lymph node dissection is required.

Confirming the Mediastinum Before Treatment: EBUS vs. Mediastinoscopy

Imaging alone is an imperfect predictor of nodal disease, roughly 15% of patients with a PET-CT-negative mediastinum (no N2/N3 uptake) are found to have positive N2/N3 nodes at surgical staging. This is why invasive mediastinal staging is frequently needed before committing a patient to a treatment plan. Two complementary techniques are used:

  • Endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS): a minimally invasive, needle-based technique that samples stations 2, 4, 7, and 10.
  • Mediastinoscopy: a surgical procedure that samples stations 2, 4, and 7.

The ASTER trial (Annema et al., JAMA 2010) directly tested a combined strategy, EBUS/EUS-FNA first, followed by mediastinoscopy only if that initial sampling was negative, against mediastinoscopy alone. The combined approach was substantially more sensitive: 79% for mediastinoscopy alone, 84% for EBUS alone, and 94% for the combined strategy. This is why current practice favors starting with EBUS and reserving mediastinoscopy for cases where EBUS is negative but clinical suspicion remains high.

Clinical Pearl Nodal disease at stations 5 or 6 with a right-sided primary tumor is automatically N3, not N2, these stations are left-sided by definition. This is a favorite staging pitfall.
Clinical Pearl Station 7 (subcarinal) is the most commonly involved mediastinal station because it drains both lungs, think of it as the "central hub" of thoracic lymphatic drainage, and expect it to be included in nearly every locally advanced radiation target volume.

Workup & Staging.title: Lung Cancer Workup & Staging
Workup & Staging.html:
Before any treatment decision can be made, a lung cancer must be worked up and staged, meaning clinicians need to know the tumor's size and local extent (T), whether nearby lymph nodes are involved (N), and whether it has spread to distant sites (M). This doc walks through how that workup is done and how the resulting information is translated into a stage.

Building the Workup: History, Labs, and Functional Status

Workup starts with a full history and physical, specifically probing for risk factors, age, smoking history, prior cancer history, family history, and occupational exposures, along with smoking cessation counseling at every visit. Baseline labs include a CBC and CMP. Because many patients are being considered for surgery, pulmonary function tests are essential: at minimum, FEV1 >40% and DLCO >40% are required for medical operability.

Imaging and Establishing a Tissue Diagnosis

Standard imaging includes a dedicated CT chest and an FDG PET-CT scan. Brain MRI with contrast is used to rule out occult brain metastases, and the threshold for obtaining it differs by histology: it is mandatory for all SCLC patients (reflecting SCLC's high propensity for brain spread), while for NSCLC it is mandatory for stage II disease (tumors >4 cm) and only optional for stage IB (>3 cm).

Tissue diagnosis is generally obtained before surgery whenever possible, via CT-guided needle biopsy for peripheral lesions, or endoscopic (EBUS/EUS) FNA for central lesions, particularly when the diagnosis is uncertain, when the patient may be a candidate for therapy prior to surgery (stage IB or higher), or when a diagnosis is needed before proceeding with SBRT in a non-surgical candidate. One notable exception: very small, high pretest-probability lesions (stage IA, ≤1 cm) may proceed directly to surgery, with an intraoperative wedge resection or needle biopsy confirming the diagnosis before a formal lobectomy is performed.

TNM Staging (AJCC 8th Edition)

NSCLC and SCLC share the same underlying TNM system. T-stage is driven primarily by tumor size, with specific cutoffs:

  • T1 ≤3 cm, subdivided into T1a (≤1 cm), T1b (1-2 cm), and T1c (2-3 cm)
  • T2 involves the main bronchus, visceral pleura, or an obstructing airway, or is 3-5 cm (T2a 3-4 cm, T2b 4-5 cm)
  • T3 5-7 cm, or invasion of the parietal pleura, chest wall, or parietal pericardium, or a separate nodule in the same lobe
  • T4 >7 cm, or a separate nodule in a different ipsilateral lobe, or invasion of the mediastinum or chest wall

N-stage follows the station map described in the Anatomy & Lymphatics doc: N0 (no nodal disease), N1 (ipsilateral hilar), N2 (ipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal), N3 (contralateral mediastinal/hilar, or supraclavicular). M-stage separates M1a (a contralateral lung nodule, pleural/pericardial nodule, or malignant pleural/pericardial effusion), M1b (a single extrathoracic metastasis), and M1c (multiple extrathoracic metastases).

Limited vs. Extensive Stage: The Separate System for SCLC

Although SCLC can be described with the same TNM system, in practice it is more often described using a simpler, radiation-therapy-oriented framework:

  • Limited stage (LS-SCLC): any T, any N, M0 disease that can safely be encompassed in a tolerable radiation plan. This typically corresponds to AJCC stage I-III, but specifically excludes T3-T4 disease when multiple lung nodules are too extensive or too large to treat safely.
  • Extensive stage (ES-SCLC): any T, any N, with M1a/b/c disease, or T3-T4 disease that is too large or extensive to treat within a tolerable radiation plan.

Notice that this definition is built around radiation deliverability, not a strict anatomic cutoff, a large, multifocal T4 tumor can be classified as "extensive stage" even without any distant metastasis, simply because it cannot be safely irradiated with curative intent.

Molecular and Biomarker Testing

PD-L1 testing is performed on tumor tissue using the tumor proportion score (TPS), the percentage of viable tumor cells showing partial or complete membrane staining. A TPS ≥1% is considered positive and determines whether immune checkpoint inhibitors are incorporated into treatment; a TPS ≥50% is high enough that checkpoint inhibitor monotherapy alone may be considered in the advanced/metastatic setting.

Next-generation sequencing (NGS) should be performed on tissue whenever possible to look for targetable driver mutations, EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF V600E, NTRK, MET exon 14 skipping, RET, HER2, and KRAS G12C are all now associated with specific targeted therapies (see the table in the Treatment Paradigms doc). If a targetable mutation is present, targeted therapy takes precedence over immunotherapy. In the metastatic setting, circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA, "liquid biopsy") can also be sampled from a blood draw and analyzed for mutations faster than a repeat tissue biopsy, but it does not replace histologic tissue diagnosis, which remains the gold standard.

Clinical Pearl Extensive-stage SCLC is not only defined by metastases, a T3-T4 tumor that is simply too large or multifocal to fit into a tolerable radiation field is also classified as extensive stage, even with M0 disease.
Clinical Pearl PD-L1 TPS ≥1% = positive (eligible for combination immunotherapy); TPS ≥50% = eligible for immunotherapy monotherapy without chemotherapy.

Imaging.title: Thoracic Imaging Pearls
Imaging.html:
Imaging drives almost every decision in thoracic oncology, from telling a benign nodule apart from a cancer, to staging the mediastinum, to planning exactly where the radiation beam should go. This doc walks through the key imaging patterns and pitfalls a sub-intern should recognize.

Characterizing the Solitary Pulmonary Nodule

Not every nodule is cancer, and CT features help estimate risk. Malignancy is favored by a spiculated margin (versus a smooth or lobulated margin, which is more reassuring), upper lobe location, size >3 cm (at which point a "nodule" is renamed a mass and treated as cancer until proven otherwise), and a doubling time less than 400 days. Contrast enhancement also helps: enhancement >20 Hounsfield units (HU) suggests malignancy, while enhancement <15 HU is highly sensitive for a benign process.

Nodule composition matters too, in a somewhat counterintuitive way: risk increases from pure ground-glass opacity (GGO) → part-solid → solid, but part-solid nodules carry a paradoxically high risk of malignancy despite often growing slowly. This reflects the natural history of lepidic-growth adenocarcinoma, where the solid component of a part-solid nodule usually represents invasive tumor while the ground-glass component represents lepidic (non-invasive) growth along alveolar septae. Two practical rules follow from this: the solid component should be measured on the lung window, not the mediastinal window, because that choice can change the T-stage in adenocarcinoma; and screening-detected nodules are triaged by size and risk-factor status (for example, a high-risk nodule >8 mm generally prompts a short-interval CT, PET-CT, or biopsy).

Histology Leaves a Fingerprint on Imaging

Squamous cell carcinoma classically arises centrally (66-90% of cases), frequently causing obstructive pneumonitis or lobar collapse from a bronchus-occluding mass. A high-yield discriminating feature: squamous cell carcinoma cavitates in up to 82% of cases from central tumor necrosis, a useful clue whenever a cavitary lung mass is on the differential. On immunohistochemistry, squamous cell carcinoma is p63-positive/TTF1-negative (the reverse of adenocarcinoma), which matters clinically because pemetrexed is less effective and bevacizumab carries a higher hemorrhage risk in squamous histology.

Adenocarcinoma, in contrast, is usually peripheral and can appear as a subsolid or spiculated nodule, sometimes with air bronchograms or pleural indentation, findings that reflect its lepidic growth pattern.

Clinical Pearl A centrally located, cavitating lung mass should raise suspicion for squamous cell carcinoma: cavitation occurs in up to 82% of cases due to tumor necrosis, making it one of the more reliable imaging discriminators between NSCLC subtypes.

The "Iceberg Sign" of Small Cell Lung Cancer

SCLC has a distinctive imaging gestalt: a central, perihilar mass accompanied by bulky mediastinal adenopathy that often dwarfs the primary tumor: sometimes called the "iceberg" pattern, where the visible tumor is only a small piece of a much larger nodal burden. SCLC is also highly FDG-avid and tends to grow rapidly, consistent with its high-grade neuroendocrine biology and its historical staging as Limited vs. Extensive rather than pure TNM.

PET-CT: Its Role and Its Blind Spots

FDG PET-CT is the standard tool for N- and M-staging in lung cancer and meaningfully changes management: it upstages roughly 20-30% of patients compared with CT alone, sparing many patients a futile thoracotomy for disease that has already spread beyond what CT could show. The traditional malignancy threshold is an SUVmax >2.5, but this cutoff is imperfect and overlaps substantially with benign, inflammatory disease. False positives include tuberculosis, fungal infection, and sarcoidosis; false negatives include carcinoid tumors, lepidic-predominant adenocarcinoma, and sub-centimeter nodules below PET's spatial resolution. This is precisely why a PET-negative mediastinum still sometimes requires invasive confirmation before treatment (see Anatomy & Lymphatics).

Pancoast (Superior Sulcus) Tumors

Tumors arising at the extreme apex of the lung, in the superior sulcus, are a distinct clinical and imaging entity. They are notorious for being initially mistaken for apical pleural thickening or scarring on chest imaging, a classic pitfall that can delay diagnosis. Because these tumors sit directly against the brachial plexus, subclavian vessels, and vertebral bodies, MRI is superior to CT for assessing invasion of these structures, and that assessment directly drives both resectability and radiation planning. On T-staging, chest wall invasion alone keeps a tumor at T3, while invasion of the brachial plexus, subclavian vessels, or a vertebral body upstages it to T4. Clinically, invasion of the sympathetic chain/stellate ganglion produces Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis.

4D-CT and Motion Management

Because tumors move with breathing, SBRT and conventional planning for lung tumors typically use a 4D-CT acquisition, which captures the tumor's position across the full respiratory cycle. An internal target volume (ITV) is then generated, often using a maximum-intensity-projection across the respiratory phases, so that the treatment volume covers the tumor wherever it moves during breathing. Motion is not uniform throughout the lung: lower lobe tumors move more than upper lobe tumors because of diaphragmatic excursion. When motion exceeds roughly 1 cm, it typically prompts additional motion-management strategies, abdominal compression, respiratory gating, breath-hold techniques, or real-time tumor tracking, rather than simply enlarging the treatment volume to cover the full range of motion.

Clinical Pearl An apical lung lesion that looks like simple "pleural thickening" or "apical scarring" deserves a second look, especially with arm/shoulder pain, hand weakness, or Horner syndrome, these are the classic presenting clues to a Pancoast tumor that is easy to miss on imaging.

Treatment Paradigms.title: Lung Cancer Treatment Paradigms
Treatment Paradigms.html:
Once a lung cancer has been staged, treatment follows a fairly predictable branching logic based on stage, resectability, and, for SCLC, whether disease is limited or extensive. This doc walks through the standard paradigm for each major disease category.

Early-Stage NSCLC (Stage I–II): Surgery vs. SBRT

  • Medically operable, tumor ≤2cm → sublobar resection (wedge resection or segmentectomy)
  • Medically operable, tumor >2cm → lobectomy (historical gold standard, preferred over pneumonectomy when feasible)
  • Medically inoperable or declines surgery, peripheral tumor → SBRT: 50 Gy/5 fx, 48 Gy/4 fx, or 54 Gy/3 fx (single-fraction 34 Gy/1 fx at some institutions)
  • Central tumor (within 2cm of a mediastinal critical structure) → SBRT requires at least 4–5 fractions, never single- or 3-fraction (risk of esophageal ulceration, bronchial stenosis, hemorrhage)
  • Resectable, tumor ≥4cm or node-positive → neoadjuvant immune checkpoint inhibitor + platinum-doublet chemotherapy before resection
  • No neoadjuvant given, ALK-positive → adjuvant alectinib
  • No neoadjuvant given, EGFR-positive → adjuvant osimertinib
  • No neoadjuvant, no targetable mutation, PD-L1 ≥1% → adjuvant immunotherapy
  • No neoadjuvant, no targetable mutation, PD-L1 <1% → platinum-doublet chemotherapy alone

Locally Advanced NSCLC (Stage III): ChemoRT and Maintenance Immunotherapy

  • Unresectable (bulky N2 >3cm, multi-station N2, or N3) → definitive concurrent chemoradiation, 60 Gy/30 fractions to the primary tumor/involved nodes only (no elective nodal irradiation) → 1 year of maintenance durvalumab (the "PACIFIC regimen")
  • EGFR-mutant → maintenance osimertinib instead of durvalumab
  • Limited, resectable N2 disease (e.g., single-station) → surgery may be considered as an alternative to, not in addition to, definitive chemoRT
  • Positive margin (R1) or gross residual disease (R2) after resection → postoperative radiotherapy (PORT)
  • pN2 with high-risk features (ECE, multi-station nodal involvement) → PORT may still be considered
  • Superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumor, resectable → induction chemoradiotherapy (cisplatin/etoposide-based, ~45 Gy) → surgical resection
  • Superior sulcus, not resectable → definitive RT to 60 Gy

Metastatic (Stage IV) NSCLC

  • Targetable driver mutation present → targeted therapy
  • No driver mutation, PD-L1 ≥1% → immune checkpoint inhibitor (monotherapy if PD-L1 ≥50%)
  • PD-L1 <1% → chemotherapy ± ICI
  • Oligometastatic disease (often ≤5 sites), favorable factors → SBRT or other local consolidative therapy to all sites; can delay the next line of systemic therapy or allow time off therapy altogether
  • Limited brain metastasis burden → SRS alone, or surgery with pre-/postoperative SRS
  • Extensive brain metastasis burden → whole brain radiotherapy
  • Symptomatic, widespread disease, good performance status → higher-dose palliative thoracic RT (≥30 Gy/10 fractions equivalent), modest survival benefit, more esophageal toxicity
  • Symptomatic, widespread disease, poor performance status → shorter palliative course (20 Gy/5 fx, 17 Gy/2 fx, or a single 10 Gy fraction)

Limited-Stage SCLC

  • Standard approach → concurrent chemoradiation: platinum (cisplatin)/etoposide with radiation starting during cycle 1 or 2
  • Preferred RT regimen → 45 Gy/30 fractions given twice daily (BID) over 3 weeks (only primary tumor/involved nodes treated, no elective nodal irradiation)
  • Cannot tolerate or declines BID treatment → 66 Gy/33 fractions once daily
  • Complete or partial response after chemoradiation → adjuvant durvalumab, continued up to 2 years
  • Complete or partial response, reasonable performance status → consider prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI), 25 Gy/10 fractions, ideally with hippocampal avoidance

Extensive-Stage SCLC

  • Standard approach → platinum-etoposide chemotherapy + immune checkpoint inhibitor (atezolizumab or durvalumab), 4–6 cycles, then maintenance immunotherapy
  • Good response, good performance status, low extrathoracic disease burden → consider consolidative thoracic RT, 30 Gy/10 fractions
  • PCI vs. MRI surveillance alone → remains an area of genuine controversy and practice variation
Clinical Pearl The 2 cm tumor-size cutoff is one of the most testable numbers in early-stage NSCLC: ≤2 cm allows sublobar resection; >2 cm requires lobectomy.
Clinical Pearl "ChemoRT then maintenance immunotherapy" is the shared architecture of modern locally advanced NSCLC (chemoRT → durvalumab) and limited-stage SCLC (chemoRT → durvalumab) treatment. Recognizing this parallel helps organize both paradigms in your memory.

High-Yield Literature.title: High-Yield Thoracic Trials
High-Yield Literature.html:
Radiation oncology is built on randomized trial evidence, and a handful of practice-changing trials define the current standard of care in thoracic oncology. This doc walks through the trials most likely to come up on rounds or on exams, organized by clinical scenario, with emphasis on why each trial changed practice.

Surgery for Early-Stage NSCLC

The LCSG trial (Ginsberg & Rubinstein, Ann Thorac Surg 1995) randomized patients with suspected cT1N0 (≤3 cm) NSCLC to lobectomy vs. limited (sublobar) resection and found sublobar resection had roughly 3 times the local recurrence risk and ~50% higher lung-cancer-related mortality, establishing lobectomy as the long-standing gold standard. Decades later, the Alliance/CALGB 140503 trial (Altorki et al., NEJM 2023) revisited this question specifically for tumors ≤2 cm and found sublobar resection noninferior to lobectomy for overall survival, disease-free survival, and locoregional recurrence (5-year OS ~80% in both arms), though with a small but statistically significant decline in FEV1/FVC after sublobar resection. Together, these two trials explain the modern size-based cutoff: sublobar resection for tumors ≤2 cm, lobectomy above that.

SBRT for Early-Stage NSCLC

RTOG 0236 (Timmerman et al., JAMA 2010) was the first multicenter prospective trial of lung SBRT, treating medically inoperable patients with an actual delivered dose close to 54 Gy/3 fractions and achieving 91% 3-year primary tumor control: establishing SBRT as a viable, effective option for inoperable early-stage NSCLC. Subsequent RTOG trials filled out the dose-fractionation landscape: RTOG 0618 confirmed similar efficacy in operable patients, RTOG 0915 validated 34 Gy/1 fraction and 48 Gy/4 fractions as alternative regimens for peripheral tumors, and RTOG 0813 established that centrally located tumors need more fractions (up to 60 Gy/5 fractions) because of unacceptable toxicity, including fatal esophageal ulceration and bronchopulmonary hemorrhage, at higher per-fraction doses. The HILUS and SUNSET trials further refined this for ultracentral tumors (within 1 cm of the proximal bronchial tree), with SUNSET identifying 60 Gy/8 fractions as a safe and effective regimen. The pooled STARS/ROSEL analysis (Chang et al., Lancet 2015) suggested SBRT might even outperform surgery in a small randomized comparison, but because the trials closed early from slow accrual, SBRT remains reserved for medically inoperable patients or those who decline surgery rather than a routine alternative to surgery.

Neoadjuvant Immunotherapy: CheckMate 816

CheckMate 816 (Forde et al., NEJM 2022) randomized patients with stage II+ resectable NSCLC to neoadjuvant nivolumab plus platinum-doublet chemotherapy vs. chemotherapy alone before surgery. Adding nivolumab significantly improved both primary endpoints, event-free survival (2-year EFS 64% vs. 45%) and pathologic complete response rate (24% vs. 2%), as well as a key secondary endpoint, overall survival (2-year OS 83% vs. 71%), without increasing toxicity. This was the first phase III trial to support neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy in NSCLC and shifted the modern standard for resectable stage II+ disease from purely adjuvant to neoadjuvant systemic therapy.

PACIFIC: The Trial That Redefined Locally Advanced NSCLC

If there is one trial to know cold in thoracic radiation oncology, it is PACIFIC (Antonia et al., NEJM 2017 & 2018). Before PACIFIC, patients with unresectable stage III NSCLC completed concurrent chemoradiation and were simply observed, there was no proven way to consolidate that response. PACIFIC randomized 709 patients who had completed concurrent chemoradiation (54-66 Gy) to adjuvant durvalumab versus placebo for up to a year. The results were striking: median PFS improved from 6 months to 17 months, and 5-year OS reached 43% with durvalumab, roughly a 10% absolute improvement in survival, a large effect size for a single added drug. This is exactly why the "PACIFIC regimen" (chemoRT → maintenance durvalumab) is now the default standard of care for unresectable stage III NSCLC. A key limitation: post hoc analysis suggested durvalumab does not benefit EGFR-mutant patients, which led to LAURA (Lu et al., NEJM 2024), a trial showing that adjuvant osimertinib instead dramatically improved PFS (39.1 vs. 5.6 months) in this subgroup, giving EGFR-mutant patients their own tailored maintenance strategy. A follow-up trial, PACIFIC-2, tested adding durvalumab concurrently (not just after) chemoRT and showed no benefit, reinforcing that the original sequential PACIFIC design remains standard.

Dose Escalation Does Not Help: RTOG 0617

RTOG 0617 (Bradley et al., Lancet 2015/JCO 2019) tested a natural-seeming hypothesis, that more radiation dose should control locally advanced NSCLC better, by randomizing patients to 60 Gy vs. 74 Gy chemoradiation (with a second randomization to ± cetuximab). The result surprised the field: dose escalation to 74 Gy led to worse overall survival (median OS 29 vs. 20 months) without improving local control, and cetuximab added toxicity with no benefit. This established 60 Gy/30 fractions as the durable standard dose and taught the field an important lesson about the limits of simple dose escalation when toxicity to the lung, heart, and esophagus can outweigh any local-control gain. A secondary analysis of the same trial also showed lower pneumonitis and lower cardiac dose with IMRT vs. 3D conformal RT, reinforcing the modern preference for IMRT-based planning.

PORT Trials: Lung ART and PORT-C

Two modern randomized trials, Lung ART (Le Pechoux et al., Lancet 2022) and PORT-C (Hui et al., JAMA Oncol 2021), tested postoperative radiotherapy for resected pN2 NSCLC and both failed to show a disease-free or overall survival benefit to routine PORT, despite reducing mediastinal recurrence, because higher-grade pneumonitis offset the local-control gain. Together they overturned older practice patterns and shifted PORT's clearest indication to positive margins (R1/R2) rather than N2 nodal status alone.

SCLC: Adjuvant Immunotherapy Arrives

Just as PACIFIC transformed locally advanced NSCLC, ADRIATIC (Cheng et al., NEJM 2024) did the same for limited-stage SCLC: after concurrent platinum-based chemoradiation, adjuvant durvalumab significantly improved both PFS (median 16 vs. 9 months) and OS (median 56 vs. 33 months) compared with placebo, making adjuvant durvalumab the new standard of care for LS-SCLC. For extensive-stage disease, two landmark trials, IMpower133 (Horn et al., NEJM 2018, adding atezolizumab) and CASPIAN (Paz-Ares et al., Lancet 2019, adding durvalumab), each showed that adding a checkpoint inhibitor to first-line platinum-etoposide chemotherapy improves overall survival, establishing chemo-immunotherapy as the new first-line standard for ES-SCLC.

Clinical Pearl Notice the pattern: PACIFIC (LA-NSCLC) and ADRIATIC (LS-SCLC) both showed that maintenance durvalumab after chemoradiation improves survival, this "chemoRT then immunotherapy consolidation" architecture is one of the most important organizing concepts in modern thoracic radiation oncology.
Clinical Pearl RTOG 0617 is a favorite exam trial precisely because it is counterintuitive: higher radiation dose (74 Gy) produced worse survival than standard dose (60 Gy), a reminder that toxicity can outweigh any theoretical local-control benefit of dose escalation.
